title: Capstone: wire production config and capture slow-query + metadata-cache evidence
description: Create mikro-orm.config.prod.ts with: structured JSON logging (logger that calls JSON.stringify), a slow-query threshold of 100ms, and metadata cache enabled (GeneratedCacheAdapter pointing to a .cache/ directory). Start the app with this config. Trigger a deliberately slow query by running em.execute('SELECT pg_sleep(0.15)') via a script or endpoint. Submit a screenshot showing TWO things visible on screen: (a) the structured JSON log line for the slow query (it must include the SQL text and the time taken), and (b) a boot log line indicating metadata was loaded from cache (on the second run). If your Postgres host does not support pg_sleep, substitute any query that takes over 100ms (e.g., a table scan on a large unseeded table).
modelAnswer:
The screenshot must show:
1. A JSON log object containing at least: { sql: 'select pg_sleep(...)', took: <number>ms, level: 'warn' } or equivalent — the slow-query path in the MikroORM logger fires at warn level when a query exceeds the threshold.
2. A second log line (from a previous or concurrent boot) showing 'Loaded metadata from cache' or similar — indicating the GeneratedCacheAdapter found the .cache/ file on startup.
If you see no slow-query log: confirm the slowQueryThreshold is set on the config (not on the driver). If the cache line is absent: run the app twice — the first run generates the cache file, the second run loads it.

title: Course synthesis — two concepts you will use at Fohlio + prior-lesson callbacks
description:
This is the capstone synthesis task. Do both parts.

Part A (synthesis, ~200 words): Name the two concepts from this course you expect to use most often in your day-to-day Fohlio work. For each: name a concrete Fohlio service or feature where you would apply it, what specific problem it solves there, and which earlier lesson's homework task made it click. Generic answers ('it's useful', 'it scales') do not count — be specific and personal.

Part B (callbacks — L3, L6, L9): Describe a hypothetical production incident at Fohlio involving all three of the following: a stale Identity Map (L3), a soft-delete filter that was accidentally disabled (L6), and a missing @CreateRequestContext() on a queue worker (L9). What data corruption or bug would result? What is the minimal fix for each of the three causes?

Submit both parts as text.
modelAnswer:
Part A (rubric): Full marks require: (1) a named Fohlio service (not 'the backend'), (2) a specific problem statement (not 'performance' or 'correctness' in the abstract), (3) a reference to a specific lesson or homework task. Example of a passing answer: 'QueryBuilder filters (L6): for the multi-tenant reporting service that produces per-client budget exports — a Filter with tenantId from AsyncLocalStorage means every query is automatically scoped without every service method adding a WHERE clause. L6 homework task 3 made this concrete when I had to handle the empty-context case.' Example of a failing answer: 'Migrations (L7) because production databases need migrations.'

Part B (model answer): Stale Identity Map (L3) — a queue worker reuses a long-lived EM, so its copy of Article is hours old; an update made by an HTTP request is invisible to the worker, which then flushes the stale state and overwrites the HTTP change. Fix: decorate the worker with @CreateRequestContext() (which also fixes cause 3). Soft-delete filter disabled (L6) — a report query accidentally calls em.disableFilter('softDelete') and surfaces deleted articles to a client. Fix: scope filter disable to a scoped EM fork, never on the global EM. Missing @CreateRequestContext() (L9) — the queue worker shares the global EM, so multiple concurrent jobs mutate the same Identity Map, causing race conditions on flush. Fix: @CreateRequestContext() on the handler method.

title: MikroORM vs Prisma at Fohlio — structured comparison with personal stakes (AI-resilient)
description:
You encountered Prisma in the NestJS course (nestjs-4-data-layer). Now compare its mental model to MikroORM's across four dimensions: (1) Unit of Work vs Prisma's per-operation approach, (2) relation loading, (3) migration tooling, (4) NestJS integration. For each dimension: state which tool wins and under what conditions, and name a concrete Fohlio service shape where that dimension would tip the decision.

AI-resilient constraint: at the end, paste your comparison into ChatGPT and ask it to summarize the winner. Then write 3 sentences explaining what the AI summary missed — specifically about your own experience with both tools across this course and the NestJS course. What nuance is invisible to an AI that has not run both tools against the same schema?

Metacognitive memo: Looking back at all 10 lessons, which homework task changed your mental model the most, and why?

title: Why does the metadata cache eliminate cold-start tax, and when does it backfire?
description: MikroORM discovers entity metadata at boot time by inspecting TypeScript reflection or decorator metadata — a process that touches every entity file, parses types, and builds an in-memory schema graph. The GeneratedCacheAdapter serializes this graph to disk so the next boot can skip discovery. Why does this matter in a serverless or container-autoscaling environment where cold starts are frequent? Then name one scenario where the cache becomes incorrect and causes a runtime error — and describe the minimal invalidation step. Answer in 5–7 sentences.
